task.description:
WF-03 Step 0.5 (registry lookup) and Step 1 (diagnose) for ISS-0440. Follow docs/agents/workflows/WF-03_issue_resolving.md's own procedures for both steps; this description states the run-specific scope.

READ STEP 00's HANDOFF FIRST (artifacts_in[0]) -- ORCH already measured five facts you would otherwise spend the step rediscovering: the linter's 8.4s runtime over 1915 files, that run(_args) at lint_handoffs.ex:233 ignores its args and always lints the whole corpus, that the H1 check itself is already CORRECT, that no hook infrastructure exists, and that git 2.50.1 supports core.hooksPath. Per HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md 1.1 these are checkable claims -- verify the ones your diagnosis leans on rather than inheriting them.

WHAT MAKES THIS ISSUE DIFFERENT, and what your diagnosis must therefore do. This is NOT a bug hunt: the defect is fully understood and documented across seven occurrences. docs/anti-patterns.md's own entry states the analysis is complete and that re-documenting is EXHAUSTED. So Step 1's usual 'find the root cause' work is already done, and your actual job is different in kind:

  (a) ESTABLISH THE REAL FAILURE SURFACE EMPIRICALLY. The issue asserts the defect is agents writing a result-word into a lifecycle field. Test that against the corpus: scan all ~1915 handoff files' git history (or the anti-pattern entry's seven named occurrences) and report WHICH bad values actually appear (PASS/FAIL/DONE/COMPLETE/other), WHICH roles wrote them, and at WHAT point in a run. If the real distribution differs from the assumed one -- e.g. it is concentrated in one or two roles, or in one step type -- that changes which of the four candidate fixes is right, and it is exactly the kind of thing nobody has checked in seven occurrences.
  (b) ESTABLISH WHERE THE ENFORCEMENT POINT CAN ACTUALLY LIVE. The issue lists four candidate options (a) tracked .githooks/pre-push, (b) ORCH lints before dispatching, (c) lint call in every role's dispatch template, (d) lint_handoffs --autofix. For each, determine empirically whether it is even VIABLE here, and say what would make it fail:
     - For the hook option: a hook only fires on hosts that ran a setup step. AC2 requires that an unconfigured host either still be protected OR have its non-setup DETECTED by an existing gate. Is there an existing gate that could detect it? Look at mix letflow.check's alias chain in mix.exs and the existing check_* tasks (check_toolchain is the obvious precedent for 'verify this host is set up correctly').
     - For the autofix option: is the mapping genuinely unambiguous? PASS/COMPLETE/DONE all plausibly mean COMPLETED, but does FAIL mean FAILED (lifecycle) or a COMPLETED step with a failing result? Get this right -- an autofix that silently converts a FAILED handoff into a COMPLETED one would corrupt the pipeline's own record of what happened, which is far worse than the violation it fixes. If any mapping is ambiguous, say so plainly; that likely disqualifies (d) on its own or restricts it to a safe subset.
     - For the dispatch-template options (b)/(c): both require the linter to check ONE file, which it currently cannot do (run(_args) ignores args). Quantify what that costs: is 8.4s acceptable per dispatch, or does a single-file mode need building first? Note there may be dozens of dispatches per run.
  (c) STATE WHAT WOULD MAKE THE FIX FAIL A SECOND TIME. Six prior mitigations were written down and all six failed, because they relied on an agent or ORCH remembering. Your diagnosis must name the specific property that distinguishes a fix that holds from one that becomes the eighth tally line. Be concrete about the failure mode of each candidate, not just its mechanism.

STEP 0.5 REGISTRY LOOKUP: search docs/issues/*.yaml for prior entries about handoff linting, schema enforcement, or this specific class. ISS-0190 (grandfathering), ISS-0191 (the linter's own origin), ISS-0196, ISS-0198, ISS-0203, ISS-0204 and ISS-0262 are all known-adjacent and are cited in lint_handoffs.ex's own moduledoc. Report whether any of them already tried and abandoned one of the four candidate approaches -- if a prior run rejected the hook approach for a stated reason, that reason is load-bearing here and must not be silently re-decided (core-directives.md's decision-record rule).

CONSTRAINTS: do NOT implement the fix (WF-03 Step 1's own rule) -- this step writes only its own handoff. Do not modify lib/ or the linter. Be careful with any experiment that touches .git/hooks or core.hooksPath on this workstation: other Letflow sessions are running concurrently against this same checkout, and a global git config change could affect them. If you need to test a hook, do it in a throwaway git worktree or a temp clone, and say which you used.

Complete the handoff with your diagnosis in result.summary and next_action 'Route to CODE-DESIGNER for fix design'. Commit it to branch feature/WF03-ISS0440-20260903.

result.summary:
STEP 0.5 REGISTRY LOOKUP. Read ISS-0190, ISS-0191, ISS-0196, ISS-0198(via ISS-0203), ISS-0203, ISS-0204, ISS-0262 in full. None rejected any of the four candidate approaches for THIS class (top-level status enum violation) -- they are adjacent infrastructure: ISS-0190 is the one-time corpus cleanup that established per-file grandfathering (never revisited as a policy question); ISS-0191 built the linter itself and explicitly scoped 'is result actually attested' out, not enforcement timing; ISS-0196/0204 are about started_at/commit-at-dispatch timing, a different field; ISS-0203 is two prose-seam typos; ISS-0262 fixed file-discovery (globbing .json only), unrelated to which values are legal. No decision record blocks a hook, ORCH-side lint, dispatch-template lint, or autofix for this class -- all four remain open. This IS a recurrence in HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md's own INV-1-shaped sense (docs/anti-patterns.md's entry documents 6 same-root-cause failures before this 7th), so severity stays at least the issue's own framing; ISS-0440 is filed MINOR but the recurrence count alone would argue MAJOR if this were a fresh filing -- noted, not changed, since severity is not this step's field to edit.

VERIFIED (not inherited) FROM STEP 00's HANDOFF: (1) run(_args) at lint_handoffs.ex:233 -- confirmed by reading the source: the body calls handoff_files() (zero-arg) at line 234, never touching the bound-but-ignored _args parameter. No single-file mode exists. (2) H1 check correctness -- confirmed at lines 411-435: @legal_statuses (line 102) is the exact 6-value enum, checked via simple membership; not the defect. (3) No hook infra -- confirmed: .git/hooks holds only *.sample files, core.hooksPath was unset on the main checkout at run start. (4) git 2.50.1.windows.1 -- confirmed via `git --version`, supports hooksPath (needs >=2.9). (5) RUNTIME CLAIM CORRECTED: Step 00 reported 8.4s over 1915 files. Re-measured three times this run: run 1 (cold, but see caveat) = 74.684s over 1917 files; run 2 (immediately after) = 8.651s; run 3 = 5.119s. The 74.7s outlier is NOT a steady-state number -- `ps aux` during run 1 showed 3 concurrent `erl` processes (this checkout has 3 other active worktrees per `git worktree list`: agent-a350015d, agent-a554838a, agent-afe31f13, evidence of the concurrent-session hazard the dispatch itself warned about). Steady-state, uncontended cost is 5-9s, matching Step 00's figure closely enough to trust it as the normal-case number -- BUT under real concurrent-host load (which this repo demonstrably has right now) it can run 9-15x slower. This matters for AC5: a dispatch-time gate sized against the 8.4s figure alone is undersized for this project's actual operating conditions.

(a) EMPIRICAL FAILURE SURFACE, from the 7 documented occurrences (docs/anti-patterns.md's 'Subagents write a handoff's top-level status field...' entry, read in full) plus this run's own git-history search: occurrence 1-3 (WF02-REQ160-20260827, PR #681): TEST-DESIGN-VALIDATOR wrote 'FAIL', TEST-RUNNER wrote 'COMPLETE', RELEASE-VALIDATOR wrote 'DONE' -- three different roles, three different words, same run. Occurrence 4 (WF02-REQ161-20260827): CODE-DESIGNER wrote 'DONE'. Occurrences 5-6 (WF02-REQ181-20260829, PR #725): SECURITY-REVIEWER and REVIEWER both wrote 'DONE'. Occurrence 7 (WF02-REQ196-20260830): TEST-RUNNER wrote 'DONE'. Occurrence 8/ISS-0440 itself (WF03-ISS0426-20260902, PR #848): ELIXIR-DEV wrote 'PASS'. DISTRIBUTION: bad-value vocabulary is {DONE: 4, PASS: 2 (this run's ISS-0426 occurrence plus the historical git-log fixes below), COMPLETE: 1, FAIL: 1} -- concentrated on DONE but not exclusively; role vocabulary spans 7 DIFFERENT roles (TEST-DESIGN-VALIDATOR, TEST-RUNNER x2, RELEASE-VALIDATOR, CODE-DESIGNER, SECURITY-REVIEWER, REVIEWER, ELIXIR-DEV) with NO single role responsible for more than 2 of 8 -- this rules out any fix scoped to 'fix role X's prompt', confirming the issue's own framing that this is systemic, not role-specific. Cross-checked against actual git history of FIX commits (git log -p for removed top-level status lines): every found historical fix commit (09dd2798, d56738cf, da0537d2) shows the SAME pattern -- PASS/DONE at top level, corrected to COMPLETED, never once to FAILED. WHAT POINT IN A RUN: always at step completion, by the completing agent itself, immediately before that agent's own handoff would be read by ORCH or by CI -- never at dispatch, never by ORCH's own authorship (confirmed: anti-patterns.md's 7 occurrences are all attributed to dispatched subagents, never to ORCH writing its own handoff; this matters for option (b), see below).

(b) VIABILITY OF THE FOUR CANDIDATES, empirically tested:

  (a) TRACKED .githooks/pre-push. TESTED LIVE in an ISOLATED CLONE (not a worktree -- worktrees share the parent repo's .git/config, confirmed the hard way: setting core.hooksPath in a `git worktree add` checkout leaked into THIS checkout's .git/config; caught immediately via `git config --local --get core.hooksPath` on the main repo returning the leaked value, reverted with `git config --local --unset core.hooksPath`, reconfirmed unset (exit 1) before proceeding -- an independent `git clone --local` was used for the remainder of the experiment instead, at C:/Users/tvolo/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/letflow2-iss0440-hooktest-clone, since removed). Scenario A (unconfigured host, default clone, no hooksPath set): committed a synthetic handoff with top-level status:'PASS' -- commit succeeded with ZERO local resistance (exit 0), exactly reproducing all 7 real occurrences' actual failure mode (caught only later, never at commit time). Scenario B (configured host, .githooks/pre-push added, `git config core.hooksPath .githooks` set LOCAL to the isolated clone only): pushed the same bad commit to a throwaway bare repo -- hook fired, ran `mix letflow.lint_handoffs`, it reported 'FAIL -- 1 new (un-grandfathered) violation(s)' citing the synthetic file by path, Mix.raise'd non-zero, and `git push` itself failed ('error: failed to push some refs'). CONCLUSION: the hook mechanism itself works and is genuinely testable/provable. BUT AC2's own question is answered negatively: an unconfigured host is not caught by anything else. mix.exs's letflow.check alias chain (read in full) has no check_* task that verifies hook setup -- check_toolchain checks Elixir/OTP/Rust version drift against .tool-versions (advisory, prints to stderr, never fails), check_requirements_registration and check_deferral_staleness both check docs/requirements.yaml content, none of the four existing check_* tasks look at git config or hook presence at all. There is no existing gate of the shape 'verify this host ran the hooksPath setup step' -- one would have to be built new, and CRITICALLY, that new check could only run inside `mix letflow.check` itself, which is exactly the CI-time gate that already exists and already catches every one of these 7 violations today (mix.exs line 105, `letflow.lint_handoffs` is already a hard step in the `letflow.check` alias, and .github/workflows/ci.yml's sole backend-gate step is literally `mix letflow.check`). So the hook option's own honest self-assessment is: it only ever helps on a host that both (i) ran setup and (ii) pushes to a real remote before CI would have caught it anyway -- a narrower window than it first appears, since CI already catches 100% of these regardless of hook presence. Its value is earlier feedback on a configured host, not a strictly larger catch rate.

  (b) ORCH LINTS BEFORE DISPATCHING THE NEXT STEP. Structurally viable: confirmed all 8 occurrences (including this run's own trigger, ISS-0426) were written by a DISPATCHED SUBAGENT, never by ORCH authoring its own handoff -- so ORCH is never the party that would need to catch itself, and 'lint every handoff I did not myself author, before dispatching the next step' has no self-referential gap. This is also literally the anti-patterns.md entry's OWN prior suggestion (Recurrence 4-6 write-ups both proposed exactly this) and it still failed 3 more times after being proposed -- because 'ORCH should remember to run this' is prose, not mechanism. The single-file cost question: run(_args) ignoring args (verified above) means today this would cost the FULL 5-9s (or worse under contention) corpus scan at EVERY dispatch boundary, not a per-file check. A run with ~13 steps (REQ-160's own file count above) would pay that 13 times = 65-117s of pure linting overhead per run at steady state, more under contention -- not fatal but non-trivial, and a genuinely single-file mode (trivial to add: filter handoff_files() to one path) would cut this to sub-second per dispatch. Recommend flagging 'build single-file mode' as a real design consideration, not a nice-to-have, since (b) and (c) both depend on it for cost to stay negligible at O(dispatches-per-run) call frequency.

  (c) LINT CALL IN EVERY ROLE'S DISPATCH TEMPLATE (i.e., the completing agent lints its OWN file before declaring done). Same cost math as (b), same single-file-mode dependency. Structural difference from (b): this requires editing the spawn prompt of every one of the ~15 role files (.claude/agents/*.md) rather than one place in ORCH's own procedure -- confirmed HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md's own §1.2 precedent (ISS-0204) that spawn-prompt content is a real, ORCH-controlled lever ('costs the other fourteen roles an instruction each removed from their spawn prompts' -- HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md line 196, describing the OPPOSITE change). Weaker than (b) on the exact failure mode observed: every one of the 7 occurrences was the COMPLETING agent itself making the mistake -- asking that same agent to self-check is asking the party that just proved susceptible to the error to also catch it, whereas (b) puts the check in a different, independent party (ORCH) reading the file fresh. (b) is structurally stronger for this specific defect shape; (c) is not disqualified but is the weaker of the two dispatch-boundary options.

  (d) --autofix MODE. THE AMBIGUITY QUESTION, resolved empirically: searched full git history (`git log --all -p -- 'handoffs/**/*.json'`) for every removed top-level status line across all fix commits found. Every historical FIX found (09dd2798: DONE->COMPLETED, PASS->COMPLETED; d56738cf: PASS->COMPLETED x2; da0537d2/ISS-0426: PASS->COMPLETED) mapped to COMPLETED, never to FAILED. Checked the one occurrence anti-patterns.md explicitly names as writing top-level 'FAIL' (TEST-DESIGN-VALIDATOR, WF02-REQ160-20260827/step-03b): the file's CURRENT/merged content (git show a0c401de, the squash-merge commit) has top-level status:'FAILED' -- correctly spelled, correct enum member, meaning it WAS fixed before merge (matching CI's own gate: mix letflow.check must pass for a PR to be mergeable at all, so no bad value survives to a merge commit). This means the FAIL case's own fix is NOT independently visible in surviving history (squashed away), so I cannot empirically confirm from git alone whether that specific instance was corrected to FAILED (lifecycle, correct if the step genuinely failed its gate) or was actually a COMPLETED step with a failing verdict that got relabeled. THE MAPPING IS THEREFORE GENUINELY AMBIGUOUS FOR EXACTLY THE VALUE THE DISPATCH FLAGGED AS HIGH-RISK: PASS/COMPLETE/DONE all safely autofix to COMPLETED (100% of independently-verifiable historical fixes agree, 0 counterexamples found) -- but FAIL cannot be mechanically mapped without reading result.status/result.verdict AND knowing whether the step's own gate genuinely failed (top-level FAILED, correct) versus the agent merely describing a failing finding while the step itself still completed its work (top-level COMPLETED, result.status still legitimately 'FAIL'). An autofix that guesses wrong on FAIL silently launders a real FAILED handoff into COMPLETED, corrupting the one field the whole pipeline's claim procedure (HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md section 1, 'PENDING' matching) and every gate/escalation count depends on -- strictly worse than leaving the violation for a human-equivalent (CODE-DESIGNER/CI) to see and fix with context. CONCRETE RECOMMENDATION: --autofix is safe ONLY for a closed, verified-safe subset {PASS, COMPLETE, DONE} -> COMPLETED, and MUST refuse (report, not silently resolve) on FAIL or any other unrecognized value, routing that case to a human-equivalent decision the same way it does today. This restricts but does not disqualify (d); it disqualifies an autofix that tries to handle FAIL.

(c) WHAT WOULD MAKE THE FIX HOLD THIS TIME, i.e. survive being the 8th tally line: every one of the 6 prior written-down mitigations (each fully documented in the anti-patterns.md entry's own recurrence log) shared exactly one property -- each relied on some AGENT (ORCH or the completing role) REMEMBERING to run a check that was not itself invoked by anything else. 'ORCH greps every handoff before dispatching' (proposed after occurrence 3, failed by occurrence 4-6), 'run mix letflow.lint_handoffs before considering a step done' (proposed after occurrence 1-3, failed by occurrence 4+), catching it from 'the wording of the subagent's own completion report' (occurrence 6's actual catch mechanism -- explicitly named in the write-up as still manual vigilance, not automation) -- all of these are PROSE instructing a future execution of an agent to perform an extra step that nothing forces it to perform. The property that distinguishes a fix that holds: THE CHECK MUST FIRE AS A DIRECT, MECHANICAL CONSEQUENCE OF AN ACTION THE PIPELINE STRUCTURALLY CANNOT AVOID TAKING, WITH NO AGENT DECISION IN THE LOOP ABOUT WHETHER TO RUN IT. Every one of the 4 candidates sits at a different point on this axis: (a) hook -- fires automatically on push, but ONLY if setup happened, and setup itself is exactly the kind of one-time agent action that can be (and evidently would be, since none exists today after 8 occurrences) skipped or forgotten; still requires an agent decision (did I configure this host) upstream, just moved earlier. (b) ORCH-lints-before-dispatch -- fires only if ORCH's own procedure document is written so that lint-then-dispatch is one inseparable mechanical step (not two steps where the second can be skipped), e.g. wired into the SAME code path/checklist item that already handles commit-at-dispatch (ISS-0196's fix, which DID hold across every run since -- because it was written into HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md section 1.3 as a canonical single procedure ORCH executes every dispatch, not a suggestion). (c) dispatch-template self-lint -- same shape as (b) but weaker per the self-checking argument above. (d) autofix -- the only candidate that requires ZERO agent memory at all once shipped, because it is not a check an agent chooses to run, it is machinery that mechanically corrects the file as part of the SAME lint invocation that already runs unconditionally in mix letflow.check (mix.exs line 105) -- meaning it inherits CI's existing 100%-of-merges enforcement for free and needs no new call site anywhere. CONCRETE VERDICT: (d), restricted to the verified-safe {PASS,COMPLETE,DONE}->COMPLETED subset, is the strongest single candidate against the 'holds a second time' test, because it is the only one with no agent-remembering step at all -- but it does not close the FAIL gap, and it does not give EARLIER feedback than CI (an agent still won't know until push/CI time under (d) alone, same as today, just self-heals instead of failing the build). The strongest COMBINATION, per the issue's own framing that CODE-DESIGNER should weigh options rather than have one prescribed: (d)-restricted (mechanical, no memory required, handles the 3 safe values with zero agent action) PLUS (b) wired as an inseparable step of ORCH's existing commit-at-dispatch mechanism per HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md section 1.3's own precedent (mechanical, catches FAIL and any other value the autofix correctly declines, still requires 'the same procedure ORCH already executes every dispatch' rather than a rememberable extra) -- this pairing has no step that depends on an agent choosing, each dispatch/lint cycle, to run a check that could just as easily be skipped.
result.next_action: Route to CODE-DESIGNER for fix design
